title: New Study Suggests Dying Sun May Disrupt Solar System Sooner Than Expected
body:
The Sun’s final act may unfold far sooner than astronomers have long believed, with new calculations suggesting that the star’s death could destabilise the entire solar system in a relatively brief cosmic interval.  By modelling how the Sun will shed a substantial portion of its mass as it expands into a red giant and later collapses into a white dwarf, researchers have found that the resulting loss of gravitational grip could fling the outer planets onto chaotic orbits, potentially scattering them into interstellar space within a few hundred million years after the Sun’s demise.

The study, published in a leading astrophysics journal, revisits the classic scenario in which the Sun, now halfway through its 10‑billion‑year main‑sequence lifespan, will exhaust its hydrogen fuel in roughly five billion years. As it transitions to a red giant, the star is expected to lose up to 30 % of its mass through powerful stellar winds. This mass loss reduces the Sun’s gravitational pull, causing planetary orbits to expand. While earlier models predicted a relatively orderly drift—Earth moving outward to a safer distance before being engulfed—the new analysis incorporates more realistic wind‑driven mass‑loss rates and the resulting perturbations from passing stars and galactic tides, painting a far more volatile picture.

One of the most striking implications is the fate of the gas giants. Jupiter and Saturn, traditionally thought to remain in stable, widened orbits, could experience resonant interactions that amplify their orbital eccentricities. The simulations show that as the Sun’s mass dwindles, the spacing between the giant planets becomes susceptible to mean‑motion resonances, potentially triggering a chain reaction that sends them on intersecting paths. In extreme cases, these planets could be ejected from the solar system altogether, becoming rogue worlds wandering the Milky Way. Even the more distant ice giants, Uranus and Neptune, are not immune; their orbits may become highly elongated, increasing the likelihood of close encounters with the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud objects.

The research also revises expectations for Earth’s ultimate destiny. Conventional wisdom held that the planet would either be swallowed by the expanding solar envelope or, if it survived, settle into a wider, cooler orbit. The new models suggest a narrower window of survival. As the Sun’s mass loss accelerates, Earth’s orbit could become increasingly eccentric, exposing the planet to severe temperature swings and heightened solar radiation during perihelion passes. While the planet is still likely to be incinerated before the Sun reaches its maximum red‑giant size, the timeline for that catastrophic event may be compressed by several hundred million years compared with previous estimates.

These findings carry broader implications for planetary system evolution across the galaxy. If our Sun’s demise can so dramatically reshape its planetary architecture, similar processes may be at work in other stellar systems, especially those around stars that lose mass more rapidly or experience stronger stellar winds. The study underscores the importance of incorporating realistic mass‑loss physics and external gravitational influences when predicting the long‑term stability of exoplanetary systems. It also raises intriguing questions about the future habitability of moons orbiting giant planets, which could become the last refuges for life in a dying system.

Looking ahead, astronomers plan to refine these models with data from upcoming space telescopes and missions that will monitor stellar mass loss in real time, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the European Space Agency’s PLATO mission. By observing red‑giant stars at various stages of evolution, scientists hope to calibrate the rates of wind‑driven shedding and better constrain the timelines for planetary disruption. While humanity’s immediate concerns remain far removed from the Sun’s distant swan song, understanding the ultimate fate of our planetary neighbourhood deepens our grasp of cosmic dynamics and may one day inform strategies for interstellar migration or the preservation of life beyond Earth.
